courses.title: Changement climatique - enjeux d'une transition vers une société faible en carbone

info.professors: M Christophe CASSEN, M. LECOCQ Franck, Mme Ameline VALLET
info.objectives: L'objectif de ce module est tout d'abord i) de transmettre un contenu scientifique articulé autour des problématiques de l'économie du changement climatique qui couvre une diversité de domaines (systèmes énergétique, ville, eau, agriculture, usage des sols) ii) de mettre en évidence les enjeux socio-économiques du problème, iii) d'identifier les controverses scientifiques majeures et les besoins futurs de recherche pour comprendre les mécanismes à l'½uvre, iv) enfin de cerner les marges de man½uvre et les modalités éventuelles de l'intervention publique. Ce module vise également à donner aux étudiants une vision intégrée des problématiques et des mécanismes qui sont au coeur de la transition vers une société bas carbone en privilégiant une démarche prospective. Dans ce but, il s'accompagnera d'une initiation à la modélisation prospective dans le domaine énergie/climat qui a pris une place importante dans les processus de décisions publics et privés. Le module s'appuie à la fois sur des ressources provenant du milieu des scientifiques-experts et des intervenants des sphères politique et administrative.
info.programme:
Au cours des dernières années, la lutte contre le changement climatique a vu une mobilisation croissante de la communauté internationale (par ex. Accord de Paris en 2015), et la multiplication des stratégies nationales de décarbonation ambitieuses dont l’horizon se tourne de plus en plus vers la neutralité carbone. Nos sociétés sont ainsi confrontées au double défi de gérer les impacts du changement climatique et les changements profonds de nos systèmes de production énergétiques, d’aménagement du territoire et de nos styles de vie pour atteindre une société faiblement carbonée. Ces transformations ne sont pas sans poser une série d’enjeux qui méritent une approche systémique et intégré : articulation entre les échelles d’action (territoire-Etat-International), faisabilité technique et aménagement du territoire, équité des actions mises en oeuvre (entre pays du nord et du Sud, entre couches de la population) et acceptabilité sociale, financement, articulation avec la protection des écosystèmes etc. Les problèmes socio-économiques qui en découlent sollicitent de nombreux champs disciplinaires, tant parmi les sciences de la Terre que parmi les sciences sociales. L’objectif de ce module, au travers d’interventions de chercheurs académiques propose d’apporter aux étudiants, dans un esprit interactif, une série d’éclairages sur les problématiques et les mécanismes qui sont au cœur de la transition vers une société faiblement carbonée en privilégiant les apports de la démarche prospective. Il vise plus particulièrement à i) transmettre un contenu scientifique pluridisciplinaire, articulé autour des problématiques de l’économie du changement climatique, ii) identifier les controverses scientifiques majeures et les besoins futurs de recherche pour comprendre les mécanismes à l’œuvre, iii) enfin de cerner les marges de manœuvre et les modalités éventuelles de l’intervention publique à différentes échelles.
Les présentations seront données en anglais.
info.exam: La validation du module s’effectuera sous la forme du traitement d’une question transversale aux différentes interventions du module.

info.objectives: • Penser dès à présent une gestion prospective de l'eau : maîtriser la ressource et sa qualité, programmer une utilisation durable, partager entre les différentes activités économiques, gérer de façon plus propre et économe les utilisations agricoles, réhabiliter l'environnement et les espaces (sols, écosystèmes, zones écologiques, plans d'eau, etc.), limiter les effets des évènements catastrophiques. courses.title: Animal motivation : why did the chicken cross the raod ?

info.prerequisites:
THIS COURSE WILL BE IN ENGLISH
"Why did the chicken cross the road?" If your answer is "Because it wanted to get to the other side", then this course is not for you. If, however, you want to know what motivated the chicken, be it internal factors such as physiological state, or external stimuli or the social context, then you might find it interesting. We are going to explore internal and external factors related to different motivational systems, and see if we can use them to modify behaviour.
info.objectives:
A Connaître : Collecter, reconnaître et décrire des situations qui montrent une interaction entre une motivation et un comportement. Nous allons baser ces réflexions sur nos expériences avec le comportement que nous connaissons tous de notre vie ou de la vie des animaux qu’on a observés.
B Comprendre : Associer les comportements avec des motivations et des circonstances, identifier des systèmes de motivation. Basé sur nos réflexions sur les comportements qu’on connaît, on va identifier une structure et décrire des systèmes de motivations pour interpréter les situations qu’on vient de discuter.
C Analyser : examiner des faits en isolant des causes, discriminer entre les différents systèmes de ail motivation, faire ressortir des hypothèses. Dans cette partie, on va regarder plus en détail les causes de certains comportements et des stratégies pour les changer (encourager, éviter etc.).
D Créer : Mobiliser les connaissances sur les systèmes de motivation pour créer un modèle de motivation, créer un plan pour diagnostiquer un problème comportemental spécifique. Ce modèle va servir à mobiliser nos connaissances pour créer un plan qui nous aide à diagnostiquer un comportement, à trouver les causes et mécanismes pour le modifier.
E Évaluer : Analyser la situation en utilisant le plan pour mettre en priorité les actions à prendre.
info.programme:
A Connaître : D’abord, on va ramasser des exemples de comportements, et leur lien avec des motivations. On va inclure nos connaissances du comportement de l’espèce humaine dans ces réflexions.Approche pédagogique : Réflexion individuelle suivi par une discussion en petits groupes, suivi par une synthèse fait par la classe entière.
B Comprendre : Dans cette partie, on va essayer d’identifier une structure dans les exemples qu’on a trouvés dans la partie A, et décrire des systèmes de motivations pour interpréter les situations.Approche pédagogique : Discussions en petits groupes, bilan en classe.
C Analyser : En regardant les systèmes de motivations qu’on a identifiés dans la partie B , on va isoler les causes du comportement et faire ressortir des hypothèses sur la modification potentielle des ces comportement. Cette analyse va inclure des stratégies de l’apprentissage.Approche pédagogique : Discussions en classe, potentiellement un cours sur l’apprentissage.
D Créer : On va créer un modèle du comportement qui nous permet d’identifier les différents aspects qui nous permettent de le modifier. Ce modèle va utiliser au moins en partie les quatre questions de Tinbergen (causation, function, development and evolution). On va créer un plan, un protocole pour diagnostiquer un comportement.Approche pédagogique : Travail en sous-groupes, bilan en classe.
E Évaluer : Dans cette phase du module, on va vérifier que notre plan nous permet à diagnostiquer un comportement bien connu (à la choix des étudiants) et à identifier des actions à prendre.Approche pédagogique : Travail en sous-groupes, bilan en classe.
E Évaluer : Analyser un cas concret d’un comportement spécifique en utilisant le modèle/plan créé par les étudiants pour proposer un plan d’action pour diagnostiquer un comportement, et pour des pistes de modification de ce comportement.Approche pédagogique : Travail en sous-groupes, présentation orale du plan d’action.

info.objectives: Game is a mathematical model of any decision situation, the result of which depends on the decision of at least two different individuals. Since such situations can be found in almost all fields related to our lives, the domain of applications of game theory is exceptionally broad and rich. It covers economics, industry, political and social sciences, transportation, warfare, biology, ethics and many other branches. Game theory not only represents an outstanding opportunity to persuade a wide audience of the importance, usefulness and even attractiveness of mathematics, it also leads mathematicians and technicians to such fields as ethology, evolutionary biology, social sciences, etc., that would otherwise remain marginal for many of them. The aim of the course is to provide the survey of game theory and its fascinating applications.

7. Antagonistic conflict, theory of matrix games

info.objectives: The goal of the course is to acquaint the students with spectral methods in the theory of linear differential operators coming both from modern physics and from classical physics, with special emphasis put on geometrically induced spectral properties. We give an overview of classical results and also recent developments in the field, and we always attempt to do this by providing a physical interpretation of the mathematical theorems.
info.programme:
Spectral theory is an extremely rich field, which has found applications in many areas of physics and mathematics.
One reason why it is so attractive on the formal level is that it provides a unifying framework for problems in various branches of mathematics, for example partial differential equations, calculus of variations, geometry, stochastic analysis, etc.

1. Motivations. Differential equations in physics. Unifying framework of spectral theory. Geometrical aspects.

2. Preliminaries. Glazman's classification of Euclidean domains. Elements of functional analysis. The point and continuous spectra. Self-adjointness. Quadratic forms. Sobolev spaces.

3. Quasi-conical domains. Location of propagating modes. Dimensional features of the Euclidean space. The Hardy inequality. Stability of matter. The crisis of classical physics and the rise of quantum mechanics. Mathematical formulation of quantum theory. Virtual bound states.

4. Quasi-bounded domains. Discrete and essential spectra. Compactness. Vibrational systems. Spectral isoperimetric inequalities. The symmetric rearrangement and the Faber-Krahn inequality for the principal frequency. Optimality of a disk in physics.

5. Quasi-cylindrical domains. Tubes.
Elements of differential geometry of curves and its moving frames. Quantum waveguides. Geometrically induced bound states and Hardy-type inequalities. Applications to nanostructure devices and stochastic processes.

info.programme:
The course includes:

• one-week on-site course in Prague (November 14 - 21) including all Athens activities

• three 2-hour lessons of on-line program (November 26 - December 2)

The participation in both parts of the course is mandatory. Please check your availability for the online sessions before applying for this course (see below).

After 1990, the nature of public spaces in post-socialist cities began to expand. With the new economic model of urban development, in addition to classic streets, squares and public green spaces in modernist housing estates, we also have gated communities, shopping centres and privately owned public spaces (POPS). Most often, POPS are part of new office and commercial projects.

At the workshop, we will discuss the nature of public space and its development and analyze some examples of POPS in Prague. In groups, students will investigate
POPS urban and architectural characteristics, the form of behavioural control, and see if and how POPS affects people and their activities in the place. At the end of the workshop, each group will present one selected POPS in Prague.

With this knowledge, in the second phase of the workshop, students will identify and describe selected POPS in the city where they are studying. They will perform a similar analysis as they learned at the Prague workshop. For the next three weeks after the Prague workshop, there will be twice-a-week a two-hour consultation at which the students will present the following outcomes:

1. identified
POPS in their city

2. explain its history and development

3. describe its urban and architectural features in comparison with the public space in the vicinity

4. describe the activities that take place in POPS and the forms of control present in POPS.

At the end of the online part of the course, everyone submits a presentation of one selected
POPS in one of the European cities. This way, we will learn about the various urban forms of POPS, forms of control and activities that take place there. We can also learn how European policies address the inclusion of the whole society in the urban space.

info.location: Ecole nationale des ponts et chaussées

info.prerequisites: Aucun
info.objectives:
L’industrie immobilière qui représente dans nos sociétés un des enjeux majeurs économiques et financiers de notre économie, est aujourd’hui en pleine mutation confrontée à de nombreuses crises et défis qui sont apparus ces dernières années, notamment la crise sociétale post-covid et le développement du télétravail et de nouveaux besoins des usagers, la flambée des prix des matériaux de construction, et surtout la crise environnementale et écologique avec la nécessité de décarboner un secteur majeur afin de lutter contre le réchauffement climatique.

L’objectif de ce cours est d’apporter les notions économiques et financières essentielles à la compréhension des marchés immobiliers résidentiels et non résidentiels.

L’industrie immobilière doit être considérée sous ses 3 dimensions économiques : à la fois comme une activité économique qui se produit (un cadre bâti), se consomme (un espace / habitat), s’échange, se finance et se gère en tant qu’actif (un actif / rendement), tout en tenant compte de ses propres spécificités et du contexte environnemental et sociétal actuel.

A l’issue de ce module, les élèves seront capables de maitriser :

- L’analyse économique et les différents indicateurs pertinents des différents marchés immobiliers (résidentiels et non résidentiels) (locatifs et actifs)

- Le comportement économique des acteurs de l’ensemble de la chaîne de valeur du l’immobilier résidentiel et non résidentiel

- Les grands enjeux de la décarbonation de l’immobilier dans l’ensemble de la chaine de valeur

- La relation entre les marchés immobiliers, financiers et fonciers

- La compréhension de la formation des prix immobiliers et des cycles immobiliers
info.programme:
Les éléments suivants seront abordés durant la semaine :

1 – Les 3 dimensions économiques de l’immobilier (production, usage, actif)

2 – Les indicateurs et l’analyse des marchés immobiliers (fonciers, investissement, locatif)

3 – Analyse macro-économique du fonctionnement des marchés immobiliers

4 – La formation des prix immobiliers

courses.title: Uncertainty Quantification in Numerical Simulations
courses.institution: Ecole nationale des ponts et chaussées

info.location: Ecole nationale des ponts et chaussées
info.otherProfessors: Guillaume PERRIN
info.prerequisites: Undergraduate-level mathematics (Years 1-3), with advanced Year-3 coursework in probability and statistics (linear algebra, optimization, distribution functions, parametric estimation, limit theorems, and confidence intervals).
info.objectives:
Uncertainty quantification is used in analysis and modeling (e.g. sources of uncertainty in a physical system), optimization and operations research (e.g. uncertainties on supply and demand in the modeling of a supply chain), vision and machine learning (processing noisy data...), or quantitative finance (financial risk management...).

Numerical simulation is an essential tool for modeling and analyzing complex systems in many scientific fields (physics, biology, chemistry, finance, economics, etc.). The expectations associated with it are multiple: better identification and control of risks, limitation of the costs of real experiments (car crash tests for example), search for cost-performance trade-offs, etc. The presence of many sources of uncertainty (on the models, their parameters, the reference measurements) nevertheless raises the question of the confidence that can be associated with the decisions and predictions provided by the simulation.

The objective of this course is to present a set of mathematical methods to model, propagate and analyze these uncertainties in numerical simulations.
At the end of the module, students will :

- know the theoretical foundations of the usual methods of uncertainty quantification;

- be able to implement these methods (using R) on concrete case studies
info.programme:
The course is composed of 10 sessions of 3 hours each. Each session starts with a 1h30 lecture, and ends with a 1h30 numerical practical works. During the last session, the practical work will be replaced by an exam.

Topics which will be dealt with are :

- Modeling of uncertainties

- Uncertainty propagation (quadrature and Monte Carlo methods)

- Sensitivity analysis
- Risk analysis

- Solving inverse problems in the presence of uncertainties

- Data filtering and assimilation

info.objectives:
Discover electricity system planning (long-term) studies, and associated models and tools :

- [Theoretically] Unit Commitment and Generation Expansion Planning optimisation problems, impact of climate change on data of these models, game-theoretic concepts related to the collective decision-making between the different European countries

- [Numerically] Simulate a realistic future European electricity system based on PyPSA (Python) framework and European Resource Adequacy Assessment (ERAA) data. "Playing" the associated collective decision-making between countries in a serious game
info.programme:
Simulate European electricity system planning (2050) in the form of a serious game. Each group of students will be responsible for designing the investment policy of a specific country, following the typical stages of such a long-term study:

1. Demand “projection”: depending on country, current electricity usages and future ones -> how much and type of “electrification”?

2. Production capacity: depending on cost and environmental targets (CO2 emissions), make a decision about Generation Expansion Planning*: new electricity production assets? Share of renewables/nuclear/thermal?

3. Network(s): after an introduction to basics of behavior/congestion aspects of networks at borders, collectively choose a scenario for future European interconnection capacities between simulated countries

4. Supply-demand equilibrium simulation: using a provided tool (based on PyPSA), schedule production to satisfy demand at minimal cost, on a European scale (Unit Commitment*). Observe main metrics: “failure”, (mean) production cost, renewable curtailment. Analyze impact of decisions made at previous stages (of items 1.-3.) on these metrics.

info.objectives:
THIS COURSE WILL BE TAUGHT AT
ENSAM IN PARIS, NOT TU DELFT.

Public transport infrastructures can be used as an extension of the electricity grid. This solution helps maximize the use of existing infrastructures, make sustainability and electrification projects possible even in congested grid areas, and minimize the energy consumption and costs of public transport systems.

The participants will learn how existing train, metro, tram, and trolleybus grids can be used to supply more loads such as EV chargers, buildings, and even construction sites, and how they can successfully integrate renewables and energy storage systems.

The course will consist of lectures, scientific papers presentations, multiple mini group projects that lead up to a final case-study group project on re-designing the existing public transport grid of a chosen city.

The course will be divided into 5 modules:

· Module 1: Introduction to public transport vehicles and grids

What are the characteristics and differences between a train, a tram, a metro, a trolleybus, an electric bus, and an IMC bus? How do they get their electrical power supply? How can we use these grids to do more and why should we?

· Module 2: Modeling of electric vehicles and grids

How can you model the power and energy demand of an electric vehicle such as a bus or a metro? How do you calculate the power flows in a traction grid? What parameters should you check when evaluating the performance of a grid?

· Module 3: Renewable sources and energy storage in traction grids

What type of renewable are suited for supplying traction grids and why not? And which energy storage technologies? What are the biggest challenges for renewables and energy storage in traction grids? How to model solar and wind systems and size them for a traction grid?

· Module 4: The transportation grid as a multi-functional grid

What third-party loads can be connected to a transport grid? What benefits are in this coupling for both the transport grid and the third-party users (and other stakeholders)? How to properly decide and size third party loads and define the techno-economic business case.

· Module 5: Pilots and practical examples of multi-functional traction grids

Pilots and examples from around The Netherlands and the world, and lessons learnt from them and how to apply them to the final case study.

We are at the dawn of a technological revolution that will fundamentally change our relationships with others and the way we live and work. These changes, in their importance, scope and complexity, will be unlike anything humanity has known until then. We do not yet know what will happen, but one thing is certain: our response must be comprehensive and involve all stakeholders at the global level: the public sector, the private sector, academia and civil society.

Technology and the industrial world will also be overturned. In this situation smart materials and intelligent processes have a special place.

Today, it is observed that smart materials are increasingly used for the realization of technologically important devices and formulations. However, due to their relative novelty, it is worth asking questions: what are smart materials, how do they work and what are their applications? The most important smart materials are:

- shape memory alloys, polymers and composite which have the capacity of recovery the initial shape after a large induced form change
- thermos-strictive materials; the materials which undergo changes upon temperature.

-
Chromogenic & Halochromic Materials which change color in response to electrical, optical, thermal or acidity

-
Magnetostrictive Materials which exhibit change in shape under the influence of magnetic field and also exhibit change in their magnetization under the influence of mechanical stress.

-
Piezoelectric materials; they produce a voltage under applied stress

By Intelligent processes we mean the additive manufacturing. Additive manufacturing technology is an advanced manufacturing technology used to make parts directly from a computer-driven program. The additive manufacturing process offers an efficient technique for manufacturing parts with complicated geometries. The materials transformed by these techniques are Metals, ceramics, polymer and composite. The fields of application are vast: medical implants, automotive products, and so on. Depending to the type of the material; there are several additive manufacturing technologies: Selective Laser Melting (SLM), Selective

courses.title: Emergence in complex systems, from nature to engineering

info.professors: Jean Louis Dessalles et Ada Diaconescu
info.prerequisites: All lectures and all materials are in English, so we expect students to be fluent in English. Lab work sessions are based on software written in Python. Mastery of the Python language is not required, but students who attend this course will be fluent in procedural object-oriented programming (Java, C++, Python or equivalent). If needed, they will get some knowledge of Python by themselves before the Athens week. Some fluency in basic mathematics (e.g optimization) is required.
info.objectives:
Insect colonies, evolving species, economic communities, social networks are complex systems. Complex systems are collective entities whose interactions lead to emerging behaviour. Though the detailed interactions between all agents are too complex to be described, their collective behaviour often obeys much simpler rules. The objective of this course is to present some of the laws that control emergent behaviour and may be used to predict it. The course will address conceptual issues, at the frontiers between biology, sociology and engineering.

Students who have a scientific curiosity for emerging phenomena in nature (evolution of species, self-organizing collective behaviour) and are interested in importing ideas from nature to engineering are welcome to this course.
info.programme:
The main topics studied in this module are:

Swarm intelligence; feedback loops; Emerging phenomena; definition of emergence; biological evolution; genetic algorithms; punctuated equilibria; scale invariance; implicit parallelism; autocatalytic phenomena; multi-scale systems;

cooperation; altruism; social signalling.

Potential applications are robotic swarms, smart grids, smart cities, autonomous car networks, ecology and biodiversity, crowd behaviour, financial markets, social norms, mob phenomena on social media, ...
info.exam:
The pedagogy consists in alternating lectures and practical work on machines. Each afternoon consists in a lab work session in which students will get an intuitive and concrete approach to phenomena such as genetic algorithms, ant-based problem solving, collective decision, cultural emergence or sex ratio in social insects.

Students are asked to use the software platform that is provided to them and to perform slight modifications. They will study emergent phenomena by themselves and develop their own personal (micro-)project.

Students will be evaluated based on the following tasks:

- Answers during Lab sessions

- Small open question quiz

- A 5 min. presentation of their personal project

- A short written description of their personal project (+ source files)

courses.title: Formal methods: formal specification and verification of systems

info.prerequisites:
Formal methods of system design means using mathematics to develop error-free systems. The mathematics needed is not complicated; it's just basic logic. The word "formal" means the use of a formal language, so that the system's operating logic can be machine checked.

This course is an introduction to the vast world of formal methods. It provides frameworks within which students can specify, develop, verify, and prove systems in a systematic, rather than ad hoc manner.

The course begins with review of propositional logic and predicate logic. Then we look at formal specifications, to cover set theoretic specification methods via B method, temporal specification via temporal logic and automata theory. The training includes both theoretical and practical parts. Each student will carry out an investigation of an existing formal verification system, applying it to a suitable problem of the student’s choice. Among possible projects will be the formal verification of problem solutions such as designing control systems, designing algorithms, or sophisticated data structures.

courses.title: A gentle introduction to quantum mathematics (Télécom Paris)

info.prerequisites:
https://perso.telecom-paristech.fr/rioul/cours/quantum-athens.html

https://perso.telecom-paristech.fr/rioul/cours/quantum/flyer-athens.pdf

This course offers a step-by-step introduction to the mathematical foundations of quantum information, starting from simple postulates within finite-dimensional systems. A central emphasis is placed on quantum measurement and its inherently probabilistic nature, from which the linear evolution of quantum states and the derivation of the Schrödinger differential equation for isolated systems can be mathematically derived.

The course then addresses more realistic scenarios involving noise or interactions with an external environment. In such settings, quantum states are described by density matrices, while their transformations are modeled by quantum channels, together with a general framework for quantum measurements.

If time permits, the course will also explore mathematical tools used to define and compare distances, divergences or similarities between quantum states, highlighting their connections with quantum channels and measurement processes.

As a prerequisite, participants are recommended to be familiar with linear algebra, complex numbers, and elementary probability theory and information theory. It should be noted that, although the course does not presuppose knowledge of Hilbert spaces, it does presuppose a fairly comprehensive knowledge of finite-dimensional complex scalar product spaces (also known as Hermitian spaces, the natural generalization of Euclidean spaces over the complex numbers). This course does not presuppose any knowledge on quantum physics but focuses on the mathematics of quantum information.

The course is intended for a broad audience of enthusiast students from all fields who wish to develop a solid theoretical understanding of the principles underlying quantum computing and quantum information.

info.programme:
The course combines lectures and hands-on computer tutorials in approximately equal proportions.

The lectures first review the theoretical foundations of the finite element method and the main components of a finite element solver. They then introduce the specific numerical difficulties associated with nonlinear problems and the corresponding incremental and iterative solution strategies.

Particular attention is devoted to the detailed modelling of plasticity and viscoplasticity, including constitutive formulation, numerical integration and coupling with the global finite element solver. Complementary lectures on contact mechanics and meshing provide a broader view of nonlinear computational mechanics and of the complete simulation workflow.

The tutorials are carried out using the commercial finite element software Z-set. They allow students to apply the concepts introduced in the lectures, analyse convergence difficulties, and test different modelling and solution strategies.

The course concludes with a two-day project carried out in small groups. With guidance from teaching assistants, students define, solve and critically analyse a nonlinear mechanics problem, potentially involving plasticity, viscoplasticity, damage or contact. This project is intended to develop both practical modelling skills and increasing autonomy in the use of nonlinear finite element methods.

courses.title: Physics and Mechanics of Random Media

info.otherProfessors: Anne-Françoise Gourgues Lorenzon, Christian Lantuéjoul, Benoit Noetinger, Yves-Patrick Pellegrini, François Willot
info.prerequisites: Basic knowledge in probability theory, physics and mechanics of solids.
info.objectives: Many solid media and materials (composites, granular media, metals, biomaterials, porous media, soils, rocks, etc.) encountered in materials sciences, geophysics, environmental sciences, energetics, hydrogeology,... display microstructures and structures of several length scales, showing often a non-deterministic disorder. A better understanding and prediction of the resulting multiscale and random nature of materials' mesoscopic and/or macroscopic properties requires a modeling approach based on a combination of probabilistic concepts with methods of physics and mechanics. The course, which aims to provide an introduction to this subject, will be given in a self-contained series of lectures and training sessions on computers. First, motivated by a review of advanced experimental techniques for the microstructure description, and by typical results involving fluctuations present in plasticity, damage, fracture, and flows phenomena in porous media, basic tools of applied probability and random processes are recalled. Then, probabilistic tools for the description random media and models together with their simulation are introduced. At the second stage, physics and mechanics of random media are presented from the standpoint of approximate solutions of partial differential equations with random coefficients. For example, linear electrostatics problems in random media are studied by means of perturbation expansion of the random electric and displacement fields, while bounds on the effective permittivitty and of elastic moduli are derived from variational principles. This approach of homogenization, which can be applied to other physical properties like the composition of permeability, or of the thermal conductivity, is illustrated by third order bounds. The third area of focus concerns the use of numerical techniques and especially FFT-based computations to provide estimates of homogenized properties of random media from Monte Carlo type simulations. Bounds and numerical techniques are then extended to non linear behaviours, like the plasticity of polycrystals. Given the importance of reliability problems in a multitude of engineering applications, several fracture statistics models (brittle, ductile, fatigue) are worked out from a probabilistic approach.

info.prerequisites:
A strong foundation in probability and statistics (cf. e.g. Jacod and Protter, Probability Essentials, 2004, Chapters 1 to 23)
Basic knowledge of the R language
info.objectives:
Extreme value theory is based on different principles than those of conventional statistics; it is designed to study and model exceptional events rather than the average characteristics of natural phenomena.

This one-week introductory course will start by presenting exploratory tools to analyze the behavior of extreme values in environmental and insurance data. This will help to motivate the basic principles of the statistical modeling of extreme values and the distributions that characterize them.

The two common approaches for assessing the risk of extreme events at a given level, i.e. the block maxima and the peaks over threshold approach, will be introduced and illustrated with real data examples. The course will then cover the non-stationary, the multivariate and the spatio-temporal extensions of the basic theory.

The R statistical software (freely available at www.r-project.org) will be used in the practicals, as it contains many easily accessible resources for studying and modeling extremes.
info.programme:
The course will be composed of lectures and practical sessions.

Lectures will include :

- Introduction to the extreme value paradigm

- Univariate extreme value theory (probabilistic framework and statistical inference with block maxima and peaks over threshold)

- Multivariate extreme value theory

- Non-stationary extreme value theory

- Spatio-temporal extreme value theory

- Current research trends and perspectives

During the practicals, the students will use dedicated packages in R to apply the concepts learnt during the lectures on real or simulated data.

info.prerequisites:
To get the most out of this course, students should have a solid foundation in the following areas:

- Linear Algebra: Matrix algebra, vector spaces, matrix inversion, trace, determinants, and positive semi-definite matrices.

- Probability & Multivariate Statistics: Joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, expectation, variance, covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions. Statistical Inference: Parameter estimation, likelihood functions, and Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE).

- Basic Calculus: Partial derivatives, optimization of functions, and multiple integrals.

- Programming Skills: Basic proficiency in R or Python for matrix manipulation, spatial data handling, and probabilistic simulation.
info.objectives: In earth sciences, natural resource evaluation, and environmental studies, probabilistic models are essential for predicting spatial phenomena and quantifying uncertainties arising from sparse sampling, measurement errors, or indirect observations. Because spatial observations cannot be considered independent, standard statistical and machine learning approaches are often ill-suited and lack interpretability. This course provides a mathematical introduction to the modeling of spatially correlated data through probabilistic methods, offering a foundational grounding in linear geostatistics and spatial statistics.
info.programme: General introduction and probability reminders. Random function models, Inference, Prediction (Kriging and simulations)
info.exam: Evaluation based on a mini-project

info.prerequisites: Notions of topology, differential calculus (differential of a function, partial derivative)
info.objectives: The first part of the course is an introduction that is designed to expose the theory of complex analysis in a short amount of time. The attempts to solve the pain points experienced by attending students over the years explain most of the deviations from standard expositions. We will skip some technical proofs (that will still be available for the most motivated students), focusing on the meaning of the different concepts. The second part of the course focuses on use cases of complex analysis in engineering. Numerous modern problems in many unrelated fields (scientific computing, image editing, signal processing, control problems) can be solved by complex analysis even though their statements have nothing to do with this theory.
info.programme:
During the first part of the course (~3 days), we will alternate 1h20 lectures with 1h20 exercise sessions.

During the second part of the course, we will focus on several applications. They will be presented as guided problems (half a day for each application), and the students will work together in small groups. The professor will regularly correct the different steps. Alternatively, extended theoretical exercise sessions could also be offered to volunteers.

Provisional schedule:

Day 1: General introduction, complex-differentiability (Cauchy-Riemann equations), holomorphic functions, line integrals, primitives, concepts of topology

Day 2: topology (path-connected/ connected sets, set operations, components), winding number, Cauchy's integral theorem, and corollaries.

Day 3: Power series (Laurent series), Zeros & Poles, isolated singularities, computation of residues, application to integrals of functions of a real variable

Day 4: Morning-Application to image editing
Afternoon- Application to control theory (Laplace transform, stability criteria).

Day 5: Morning-Application to signal processing.
Afternoon-Exam + debriefing.
info.exam:
Three short quizzes will be proposed during the week. They will count for 50% of the final mark. The questions will be straightforward applications of the definitions seen during the class.
A final exam will take place on the last afternoon. It will count for 50% of the final mark.

info.otherProfessors: Eric NARDON
info.prerequisites:
This course requires fundamentals in:

• Electromagnetism – electric and magnetic field, Maxwell’s equations, electromagnetic waves and Lorentz forces on charged particles

• Fluid dynamics – fluid flow, viscosity and conservation laws will be helpful in grasping magnetohydrodynamics concepts

• Python programming – notably using scientific packages numpy, scipy and matplotlib
info.objectives:
The current global context sees a revival of the interest in nuclear fusion for energy production. The decade-ongoing ITER project is now being competed by Chinese domestic tokamaks BEST (expected for
2027) and CFETR (construction started in 2020). Numerous private companies across the world are also leading researches in novel architectures of compact fusion tokamaks, leveraging the properties of new high-temperature superconducting materials. Commonwealth Fusion Systems is for example claiming a beginning of the operation on their compact SPARC tokamak in late 2026.

This one-week introductory course aims at giving the participants a basic understanding of the techniques envisioned and the challenges associated with the production of energy through nuclear fusion.

The course will cover both the basic physics of plasmas and the technological and engineering aspects of fusion reactors. It will be heavily focused on nuclear fusion achieved through magnetic confinement and on the tokamak architecture, as it they constitute today the most technologically mature path towards fusion. It will nevertheless brush on the diverse alternate strategies and machine designs that are currently being explored.

The theoretical lectures will be complemented by a practical group project. The students will be guided through the conceptual design of a tokamak, from the plasma characteristics, to the simulation of the magnetic field and the mechanical stresses in the reactor structure. This practical part will rely on analytical 0D calculations and numerical simulations using Python and open-source software.
info.programme:
The course will be composed of theoretical lectures on the following topics:

• An initial introduction to the stakes of nuclear fusion as an energy source for the future

• A physics section devoted to hot magnetized plasmas, covering most notably:

• The magnetohydrodynamics notions of equilibrium and stability

• The transport and confinement of plasmas.

• An engineering section focusing on the most widespread architecture of fusion reactor, the Tokamak, and highlighting its key technological components:

• Superconducting coils for magnetic confinement;

• Plasma heating components;

• Tritigenic covers for in-situ 3H production;

• Extraction of heat and particle fluxe

• An overview of alternative designs for nuclear fusion reactors.

The students will also participate in a group project with the aim of designing a tokamak reactor from a prescribed specification. The conceptual design will involve using analytical and numerical calculations using Python and the open-source magnetic simulation software RAT.
info.exam: The course will be graded through a combination of a final exam on the theoretical knowledges and the continuous evaluation of the practical group project.

info.prerequisites:
The course combines theoretical and empirical insights, drawing on both seminal contributions and recent research in the field.

While lectures include some light formalization, the content remains fully accessible to students enrolled in the program. No specific prerequisites are required beyond a basic understanding of economics.
info.objectives:
This course explores how digital platforms operate, compete, and innovate in today's economy. Applying concepts from managerial economics and strategy, we examine the distinctive features of platform-based markets, particularly two-sided markets, and how they shape firm behaviour, competitive dynamics, and innovation patterns.

The course combines theoretical foundations with recent empirical findings and real-world case studies. Topics include network effects, pricing strategies, platform governance, competitive interactions within and between platforms, and the impact of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and data-driven innovation.

By the end of this course, course participants will be able to:
(i) understand the economic foundations of two-sided markets and digital platforms,
(ii) analyse pricing, differentiation, and market entry strategies in platform settings,
(iii) evaluate competitive dynamics between platforms and complementors,
(iv) assess the role of platform design and governance in shaping ecosystem outcomes and
(v) explore how AI and Big Data influence strategic decisions in platform markets.
info.programme:
Course structure

*Day 1*: Foundations: Understanding two-sided markets

We begin with covering the economic logic behind platform markets, discussing network effects, pricing structures, and adoption dynamics. Cases: (i) From disruption to decline? The rise and fall of Skype, (ii)
Piggybacking: Facebook’s integration of Instagram.

*Day 2*: Platforms' strategic tools: Pricing and differentiation

We explore how platforms design pricing structures and differentiate themselves, leveraging their complementor (and user) installed bases. Cases: (i) From couchsurfing to luxe: Airbnb’s differentiation strategies, (ii)
Playing for keeps: exclusive content and rivalry in the gaming industry.

*Day 3*: Competition within and across platforms

We investigate competition both between rival platforms and within ecosystems - especially between platforms and complementors. We also discuss recent and important competition policy issues. Cases: (i) Operating system wars: How Apple and Google claimed the mobile world, (ii) An Epic entry:
Competition in the digital video game market.

*Day 4*: Innovation in platform ecosystems

This session focuses on platform-enabled innovation, and complementors strategies. We will also study how platforms can foster (or hinder) innovation in their own ecosystems. Cases: (i) Apple’s App Store: Control, ratings, and innovation incentives, (ii) Creating under constraints: How
YouTube’s rules shape innovation by content creators.

*Day 5*: When platforms learn: AI, big data, and the future of strategy

We conclude with a discussion on how AI and Big Data reshape value creation, competition, and governance in digital markets. Cases: (i)
Disruption by design: AI and the future of app stores, (ii) Feeding the algorithm: Data strategy at Amazon and TikTok.
info.exam:
Assessment: (1) Attendance to the class, 50% of the grade. (2) Group work, 50% of the grade.

Group work will take place during the afternoon sessions, in which participants will collaborate on case studies. For each case, one group will be randomly selected to deliver a short presentation to the class. However, all groups are expected to prepare presentation slides for both cases. Slides must be submitted to the instructor at the end of each session. This preparation and submission form part of the overall grade.

courses.title: Artificial Tissues and Organs
courses.institution: National University of Science and Technology Politehnica Bucharest

info.location: National University of Science and Technology Politehnica Bucharest
info.otherProfessors: Assist. Prof. Cucuruz Andreia
info.prerequisites:
The course integrates the understanding of bio & nanomaterials, engineering biomaterials for tissue engineering and regeneration, biocompatibility methods as alternative to animal testing, and medical signals & bioelectromagnetism.

The first part introduces nanomaterials & biomaterials, with a special focus on their tissue-inspired character, and their engineering and 3D printing for tissue repair and regeneration. The bone tissue engineering introduces the biological foundations of bone regeneration, with a focus on ectopic bone formation and the stimuli that drive this process.
A complementary perspective will highlight decellularization as a method to obtain scaffolds preserving native biological cues, providing functional environments for bone tissue engineering.

Participants will examine decellularized tissues as models of scaffolds retaining intrinsic biological signals and morphological features. The activity continues with a visit to the computed tomography laboratory, where bone formation is validated through 3D imaging of previously engineered models.

The introduction in alternative methods to animal testing offers a presentation of biological evaluation of medical devices, focusing on replacing in vivo animal testing with other methods such as 3D cell cultures and organoids. The practical work is an introduction to basic cell culture procedures applied to the biocompatibility assessment of medical devices. Different methods for 3D cell cultivation will be practiced.

The course continues with a presentation of monitoring equipment and characterization of medical signals. Finally, the course introduces Lower Limb
Prosthetics as a clinical application of tissue engineering and biomedical principles. It provides an overview of anatomy, biomechanics, and prosthetic design, exploring different types of lower limb prostheses, fitting techniques, and materials used in fabrication. Practical sessions emphasize hands-on applications such as alignment, gait training, and patient-centered adjustments, allowing participants to directly apply theoretical knowledge in real clinical scenarios.
info.objectives:
The course on Artificial Tissues and Organs aims to guide the students in a journey in the interesting field of engineering biomaterials, additive manufacturing, biocompatibility screening for tissue engineering, and medical signals for personalized medicine. courses.institution: National University of Science and Technology Politehnica Bucharest

info.location: National University of Science and Technology Politehnica Bucharest
info.otherProfessors: Dr.Math. Crina Narcisa Deac, Impromedia Ltd, Bucharest Dr. Eng. Gicu Calin Deac, Impromedia Ltd, Bucharest
info.prerequisites: Basic programming knowledge is recommended. No prior blockchain experience is required.
info.objectives:
This course introduces students to the fundamental concepts and practical applications of blockchain technology, with a focus on Bitcoin, Ethereum, smart contracts, decentralized applications and trust-based digital systems.

The course starts from the problem of trust in distributed systems and explains how blockchain combines cryptography, distributed ledgers and consensus mechanisms to create transparent, auditable and tamper-resistant digital records. Students will first study the basic principles of blockchain and Bitcoin, then move toward Ethereum, wallets, transactions, gas, smart contracts and decentralized application architecture.

The course has a strong practical orientation and is structured in two parts. During the face-to-face week, students will create a test wallet, perform a transaction on an Ethereum test network, use Remix IDE, write and deploy Solidity smart contracts, and work in teams to design a minimal blockchain-based prototype for a real-world scenario.

During the online follow-up, students will extend the smart contract prototype toward a simple decentralized application by connecting the contract to a web frontend using ABI, contract address, MetaMask and a web3 library such as ethers.js.
This second part helps students understand how a smart contract becomes part of a complete application flow, from user interface to wallet interaction and blockchain execution.

The course is designed to be interactive and application-oriented. Students will discuss when blockchain is useful, when it is not appropriate, and how it can be applied in domains such as industrial systems, product traceability, digital certificates, maintenance logs, audit trails and decentralized applications.
info.programme:
The course consists of 80 hours and is structured in two parts:

• Part I: 35 hours face-to-face at University Politehnica of
Bucharest;

• Part II: 40 hours online follow-up.

The face-to-face part consists of interactive lectures, guided demonstrations, practical blockchain exercises and a Remix-based team prototype. Students will study blockchain foundations, Bitcoin, cryptography, Ethereum, wallets, Remix IDE,
Solidity and smart contract development.

The face-to-face part ends with a team-based Remix smart contract prototype. The online follow-up continues the practical work developed during the face-to-face week through an individual frontend integration task. Each student connects a smart contract to a simple web interface and demonstrates basic decentralized application interaction using ABI, contract address, MetaMask and ethers.js.

Part I

Day 1: Blockchain Foundations and
Bitcoin

Introduction to blockchain technology. Trust problems in distributed systems. Immutability, decentralization, transparency and consensus. Centralized versus decentralized architectures. Byzantine Generals Problem. Bitcoin genesis and peer-to-peer value transfer. Transactions, blocks, miners, Proof of Work and the UTXO model.
Practical blockchain explorer activity.

Day 2: Cryptography, Wallets and
Ethereum + first Remix contact

Hash functions, public/private keys, digital signatures and transaction integrity. Difference between signing and encryption. Wallets, seed phrases and blockchain addresses.
Ethereum accounts, transactions, nonce, gas and transaction lifecycle.
Introduction to smart contracts, ABI, bytecode and the Ethereum Virtual
Machine. Practical activities: MetaMask wallet, Sepolia test transaction and first contact with Remix IDE through a very simple smart contract.

Day 3: Gradual Solidity lab +
CertificateRegistry TODO

Gradual introduction to Solidity and Remix
IDE through simple smart contract examples. Students will study contract structure, state variables, functions, visibility, constructor, msg.sender, require, modifiers, events, structs and mappings. The session progresses from simple contracts to a guided teacher demo of a certificate verification smart contract. Students then complete a TODO version of the contract and test it in
Remix.

Day 4: Team Blockchain Prototype

Students work in teams to adapt the smart contract pattern studied on Day 3 to a real-world use case. Possible directions include document/certificate verification, product or asset registry, and maintenance/inspection logs. Teams define actors, on-chain data, off-chain data, access control, verification logic and demo steps. The prototype is implemented and tested in Remix.

Day 5: Face-to-face prototype demo

Teams finalize their smart contracts, prepare a short presentation and demonstrate their prototype in Remix. Each team explains the problem, the blockchain relevance, the smart contract design, the data model, the verification logic, the limitations and possible future improvements.

Practical Activities

The practical part includes:

• blockchain explorer analysis;

• MetaMask wallet creation;

• Sepolia test transaction;

• Remix IDE introduction;

• Solidity smart contract development;

• guided TODO smart contract exercise;

• team-based prototype implementation;

• face-to-face Remix demo and presentation.

Face-to-Face Prototype Assessment

The face-to-face part ends with a team project presentation and Remix-based prototype demonstration. Each team must submit:

• a short presentation;

• one Solidity smart contract;

• a Remix demo scenario;

• a short explanation of the blockchain use case, actors, on-chain/off-chain data and limitations.

Part II

Online Follow-up: From Smart Contract
Prototype to Simple DApp

The online part consists of 40 hours and continues the practical work developed during the face-to-face week. Students will learn how a smart contract can be connected to a frontend and how users interact with blockchain applications through a wallet.

The online follow-up is organized into five modules of approximately 8 hours each.

Online Module
1: From Smart Contract Prototype to DApp Architecture

Students review the Remix-based smart contract prototype and study the architecture of a decentralized application. The module introduces the relationship between frontend, wallet, provider, smart contract and blockchain. Students learn the role of the ABI and contract address and understand the difference between read-only calls and state-changing transactions.

Practical activity: students prepare the structure of a simple frontend and identify the
ABI and contract address required for interaction with their smart contract.

Online Module
2: Frontend Connection with MetaMask and ethers.js

This module introduces wallet connection from a web interface. Students learn how MetaMask exposes a blockchain provider, how to request user accounts, how to check the connected network and how to create a contract instance using ethers.js.

Practical activity: students implement a simple Connect Wallet button, display the connected address and call read-only smart contract functions from the frontend.

Online Module
3: Sending Transactions from the Frontend

Students learn how a frontend sends transactions to a smart contract. The module explains the role of the signer, MetaMask confirmation, transaction hash, transaction receipt, gas and basic error handling.

Practical activity: students implement frontend forms for calling state-changing functions such as issuing a document, registering a product or registering an inspection record. They also implement revoke, deactivate or invalidate operations depending on their chosen project.

Online Module
4: Events, Logs and User Interface Feedback

This module explains how smart contract events are used by decentralized applications for audit trails and user interface feedback. Students study the difference between contract storage and transaction logs and discuss what data should be stored on-chain and what data should remain off-chain.

Practical activity: students improve their frontend by displaying transaction results, emitted events or updated verification status after a transaction is confirmed.

Online Module
5: Final DApp Integration and Presentation

Students finalize their mini-DApp, test the interaction between frontend, wallet and smart contract, and prepare the final presentation. The final demo must show a complete user flow: wallet connection, smart contract interaction, state-changing transaction, verification/read function and explanation of emitted events or results.
Practical activity: final project integration, debugging, presentation preparation and final online demo.

info.objectives:
Every catastrophe can also be viewed positively as an opportunity to learn, to embrace its anticipation, and to navigate it with resilience—provided society is prepared for it. Today, it is essential for cities worldwide to face the impacts of global warming, whether directly or indirectly. Many European capitals and major metropolitan areas have experienced seasonal floods and droughts, and Milan is no exception. While the city may not currently appear to be on the front lines of this crisis, it possesses the potential to become a leader in resilience.

This course offers an opportunity to examine the key factors of global warming and to explore Milan's responses and strategies at both public and institutional levels, considering relevant collective and individual decisions and actions, whether significant or not, from diverse and interdisciplinary perspectives. The course will specifically critique the evolution of Milan over the last 25 years within the context of sustainable and resilient scenarios. More importantly, it encourages students to investigate the daily lives of Milanese residents to identify behavioral changes that promote responsible collective and individual sustainability and resilience. In this sense, the course adopts an anthropological approach to urban settings, life, and their citizens.

Students in small groups will work on a short research (visual and/or textual) essay to be agreed upon with the professor. The subject will be related to contemporary Milan's response to global warming, with a specific focus on daily routines. It will include research, images, and/or short movies. The evaluation will consider both the quality of the research work and its presentation by each group.

Students will conceptualize a critical reflection and formulate a hypothesis about the target group(s) they are studying. The steps of investigation and documentation will be planned with the professor. The student will represent, through graphic work, the outcomes of the research essay. The graphic and scientific quality of the work will also be taken into consideration in the evaluation.

Data-driven decision-making is becoming a crucial skill to deal with engineering systems that generate vast amounts of data from the automation system. This module aims to provide students with an understanding of the general concepts, advantages and limitations of Data-Driven methods for engineering applications.

This course covers methodologies necessary for inferring useful information and identifying underlying patterns from raw, incomplete, noisy and corrupted data that is present in real-life engineering applications. This is achieved by introducing concepts and methods used to model a wide range of systems based on available data.

The module will also provide the students with the opportunity to explore advanced solutions of data analytics such as nonlinear models, model selection and error estimation.

On completion of the module the student is expected to be able to achieve the following Learning Objective (LO):

· LO1: Describe a number of models for supervised, unsupervised inference from data. Critically evaluate statistical analysis. Critically assess the fit of statistical models.

· LO2: Assess the strength and weakness of each of these models, interpret the mathematical equations from linear algebra, statistics, and probability theory used in the learning models.

· LO3: Implement efficient learning algorithms in the MATLAB language, applied to engineering problems.

· LO4: Design test procedures in order to evaluate the model hyperparameters (model selection) and its error (error estimation). Develop an appropriate experimental research design for an engineering case study considering practical limitations.

info.prerequisites:
Background knowledge: basic bridge engineering and structural dynamics.
Equipment required: Personal laptop (some practical exercises will use open-source computer programs to analyse the response of bridges under wind actions).
info.objectives:
This course focuses on the response of bridges subject to wind actions. The objectives are:

1. To gain knowledge on basic wind engineering concepts such as the atmospheric boundary layer, bluff aerodynamics and vortex shedding.

2. To describe the wind field around the structure based on current codes of practice and to understand the result of algorithms that generate three-dimensional turbulent wind velocity signals.

3. To understand the methods currently used to define the aerodynamic effects in bridge structures, including wind tunnel testing and computational fluid dynamics.

4. To use state-of-the-art models to describe quasi-static, buffeting, and aeroelastic actions in bridges.

5. To learn how to assess the comfort and stability of bridges under wind actions, including vortex-induced vibrations, divergence and flutter.

6. To understand the design concepts used in modern long-span bridges to resist wind actions.
info.programme:
Unit 1: Introduction to Wind
Engineering (2 hours)

• Course presentation. Objectives. Content.

• Introduction to wind engineering. General concepts. Wind problems in civil engineering structures. Static and dynamic effects. Methods of study.

• Description of the proposed bridge case study to be considered in the course.

Unit 2:
Atmospheric Wind (3 hours)

• Physical description of atmospheric wind. Characteristic dimensions of atmospheric wind. Global circulation, geostrophic wind, and gradient wind. Terrestrial boundary layer. Atmospheric turbulence. Local effects.

• Statistical description of the wind. Probability distributions. Extreme statistics (maximum speeds and dynamic pressures). Statistical description of turbulence.

• Regulations and standards in wind engineering. Wind models in calculation codes (Eurocode EN1991-1-4, ASCE/SEI 7-22, and AASHTO). Similarities, differences, and illustrative examples.

• Synthetic wind models. Shinozouka method. Skew angle effects.

• Exercise: study of simulated wind fields in the proposed bridge case study (practical session in class while students use their personal laptops).

Unit 3: Introduction to Aerodynamics (3 hours)

• Basic concepts of aerodynamics. Aerodynamics of blunt bodies. Reynolds and
Strouhal numbers. Vortex shedding.

• Quasi-static loads on structures. Wind pressure. Aerodynamic interference and shielding phenomena.

• Aerodynamics of bridges. Wind problems in bridges. Wakes from pylons/barriers.

• Estimation of wind loads with calculation codes (Eurocode EN1991-1-4, ASCE/SEI 7-22, and AASHTO) (Practice).

Unit 4: Dynamic Phenomena in
Structures and Bridges (3 hours)

• General response of a structure to atmospheric wind. Aeroelastic phenomena in structures, specifically in bridges.

• Aeroelastic instabilities. Vortex-induced vibrations (VIV). Torsional divergence.
Galloping. Flutter. Buffeting.

• Aeroelastic phenomena in bridges: VIV and cable galloping.

• Analysis of aeroelastic phenomena with calculation codes (Eurocode EN1991-1-4,
ASCE/SEI 7-22, and AASHTO). Scope and limitations. Illustrative examples.

Unit 5: Wind Tunnel Testing in Wind
Engineering (3 hours)

• Introduction to experimental aerodynamics. Aerodynamic tunnels. Similarity laws.
Simulation of the atmospheric boundary layer.

• Types of tests on civil engineering structures. Bridge tests.

• Specifications, requirements, scopes, and limitations of wind tunnel testing. Applicable standards.

• Interpretation and use of wind tunnel results. Examples and case studies.

• Technical visit to the wind tunnel facilities at the IDR institute (UPM campus).

Unit 6: Computational Fluid Dynamic
Analysis in Bridge Engineering (4 hours)

• Introduction to computational fluid dynamics (theory delivered in class).

Unit 7: Dynamic Analysis of Bridges
Subject to Turbulent Wind Actions (7 hours)

• Frequency-domain analysis and flutter derivatives (theory delivered in class).

• Time-domain analysis and buffeting theory (theory delivered in class).

• Linear unsteady models.

• Analysis of the dynamic response of the bridge case study subject to the wind simulated in Unit 2, and using the sectional properties obtained in Unit 6 (practical session in class while students use their personal laptops).

Unit 8: Assessment of Bridges
Subject to Wind Actions (2 hours)

• Comfort assessment and vortex induced vibrations (theory delivered in class).

• Deck stability analysis. Calculation of the critical wind speeds for the bridge used in the case study during the course (practical session in class while students use their personal laptops).

Unit 9: Design of Long-span Bridges to Resist Wind Actions (3 hours)

• Deck and pylon cross-sections (theory delivered in class).

• Passive, semi-active, and active devices to control wind-induced vibrations.

info.objectives:
Heritage represents the legacy of our ancestors, preserved for the benefit of future generations. These cultural legacies can be tangible -such as writings, art, photographs, films, artifacts, monuments, landscapes or buildings, or intangibles, including folklore, traditions, languages or customs. Together, this forms a constant, complex and multifaceted process of relationships, in which each era contributes its contemporaneity by transforming and reconfiguring the process: planning with and in heritage, not as an inert material, but as an operating system. Only from the knowledge, this valuable inheritance also constitutes an opportunity of our time to contribute, as far as possible, to its appreciation. We are not merely ob- and con-servers, but active participants in the memory of our present.

Architecture is a determining factor in the materialization, and support, of contemporaneity: working with the pre-existing, from the existing to generate a projected reality, of the future. The actions will have their seed in virtual on-site experimentation in situ with the cultural legacy on which they are founded, as well as in the place of intervention. Their codification will be the basis on which to generate architectural alternatives.
These pro-active architectural proposals can be approached from different project perspectives, promoting mechanisms of heritage conservation and activation through the coordination of international cooperation with local actions.

Students enrolled in the course will interact with cultural legacy through the web-based exploration of paradigmatic buildings.

Go deep for two weeks in the intervention city will allow you to get in touch with the immense local heritage through various virtual tours, contact with neighborhood associations, attendance at specific conferences, presentations with professionals of recognized prestige. The aim of the actions will be to promote progress in the social and cultural habitat. Within the framework presented by the UN Agenda 2030 for Sustainable Development, “Transforming our world”, orienting its objectives through the five P’s: Planet, People,
Prosperity, Peace, Partnership.
info.programme:
Cities, being large accumulators built of people, are places full of opportunities for intervention. The main objective will be to improve the urban heritage as a complex and multifaceted magma of material and immaterial elements. A view of architecture, not only as building but also looking at flows that activate habitat spaces, public spaces, sociability spaces, exchange spaces, political spaces, everyday life spaces, ambiguity spaces, contradictory spaces or intermediate spaces.

The workshop entitled Voids &
Condensers: Updating Heritage Areas [Madrid]; alludes to a semantic paradox: vacuum strategy versus condenser accumulation. We address the public space as a place of negotiation, spontaneous social representations, tribunes for demonstrations and demands, scenarios that can be reprogrammed according to circumstances, temporary supports for citizens’ movements, urban showcases of contradictory society, accumulators of layers of collective memory.

We will work in Madrid, a town of remote origins in the vicinity of the Manzanares River. Its peak was in 1561, when
Philip II moved his court from the nearby city of Toledo to the Real Alcázar in
Madrid. Declared capital until our days, it was to undertake successive enlargements absorbing and transforming itself according to the specific historical moments. The place of intervention will be a paradigmatic scenario, a public space representative of the city, a vacuum, a condenser: Madrid’s Plaza Mayor.

info.objectives: Acoustics is a branch of physics and technology related to the sense of hearing. In this course hearing and sound perception will be discussed with reference to physical characteristics of sound, properties of wave propagation, and procedures of sound measurement and analysis. Lectures will cover various dimensions of sound perception (loudness, pitch and time phenomena, binaural hearing), certain hearing models, measurement parameters specifically designed to represent perceived attributes of sound, and basic measurements for predicting the perceptual quantities. A part of the course will be devoted to practicum in acoustical measurements.
info.programme:
Hearing System

Structure: external and middle ear, inner ear, basic physiological mechanisms of hearing, Hearing: absolute thresholds, masking patterns, forward masking, frequency selectivity and masking, the concept of auditory filter, loudness, equal loudness contours, scaling of loudness, nonlinear distortion, temporal processing in the auditory system, pitch perception, timbre perception, localization of sounds, binaural unmasking, models of auditory perception Noise: basic requirements of noise control, some effects of noise on man, hearing loss, hearing aids.

Acoustical measurements

General: Fundamental acoustic quantities, sound wave propagation, waves and vibrations, Sound measuring instrumentation: microphones, calibration, sound level meters, spectrum analyzers for acoustic signals, Measurements: sound pressure level measurements, sound intensity measurements.

Psychoacoustical measurements: methodology of psychoacoustical measurements, signal presentation paradigms, adaptive methods, signal detection theory in psychoacoustical measurements.

Practicum

It is expected that the practicum will include measurements of perceptual attributes of sound (e.g. absolute hearing thresholds, masked thresholds). The lecture includes a presentation of the acoustical measurement equipment such as measurement microphones, sound level meters and spectrum analyzers. Visits to acoustical/sound engineering laboratories are also foreseen.

Suggested references

• W. Hartmann: Signals, Sound, and Sensation; Springer, 1997.

• J. Blauert: Communication Acoustics; Springer 2005.

• D. R. Raichel: The Science and Applications of Acoustics; Springer , 2000.

• D. C. Emanuel, Tomasz Letowski: Hearing Science; Lippincott, Wiliams and Wilkins; 2009.

courses.title: Smart & Sustainable: Functional Materials for the Future

info.address: Faculty of Materials Science and Engineering, Wołoska 141 Street, Warsaw, Poland
info.otherProfessors: Anna Boczkowska, Dariusz Oleszak, Jerzy R. Sobiecki, Jarosław Mizera, Joanna Zdunek, Kamila Sałasińska, Jarosław Ferenc, Emilia Skołek, Rafał Wróblewski, Bartosz Michalski, Piotr Maj
info.prerequisites: Basic knowledge of engineering, physics and mathematics.
info.objectives:
This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of functional materials, focusing on their design, synthesis, characterization, and application in modern technologies. Participants will explore nanostructured, smart, and sustainable materials and learn how these materials contribute to innovation in areas such as energy, electronics, healthcare, and environmental protection. Through lectures, case studies, lab demonstrations, and a hands-on group project, students will: gain foundational knowledge of the classification and behavior of functional materials; understand advanced manufacturing techniques including thin-film deposition and 3D printing; explore the role of materials in addressing sustainability challenges, including recyclability and eco-design; develop practical skills in material characterization (e.g., SEM, XRD, electrical measurements); learn to evaluate the suitability of materials for specific applications; collaborate in multidisciplinary teams to design material solutions for real-world problems.
By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess and contribute to the development of next-generation materials in both academic and industrial contexts.
info.programme:
The course is structured over five intensive days, combining theoretical foundations with practical, application-oriented activities. Each day focuses on a specific aspect of functional materials: Day 1: Introduction to Functional Materials & Nanostructured Systems (Overview of definitions, classifications, and key applications (e.g., sensors, solar cells, implants etc.). Introduction to nanostructured and smart materials, including shape-memory alloys, piezoelectric materials, self-healing systems, and 2D materials like graphene).
Day 2: Sustainable and Future-Oriented Materials (Exploration of eco-friendly and recyclable materials. Emphasis on green materials, biodegradability, biocompatibility, and sustainable design principles, LCA).
Day 3: Advanced Manufacturing Techniques (Focus on thin-film technologies (PVD, CVD) and additive manufacturing. Hands-on demonstrations of 3D printing of functional materials such as conductive polymers, metals and alloys).
Day 4: Materials Characterization (Laboratory-based sessions covering scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), electrical property measurements etc., and data interpretation).
Day 5: Group Project and Presentations (Students work in teams to design a material for a selected application area, integrating concepts from the course. Results are presented and peer-reviewed. Students will also defend their results before a panel composed of all course instructors).
The programme is designed to be interdisciplinary and interactive, fostering both technical knowledge and soft skills such as teamwork, critical thinking, and communication. The activities include lectures, seminars, laboratories each day of the course.
info.exam: The course will be completed based on the presentation of project results developed from a selected case study — with topics related to functional materials. Students will defend their results before a panel composed of all course instructors.
